_comment: Lighthouse CI for a NO-BUILD, noindex, invitation-gated static site.
This config previously audited nothing at all: .github/workflows/lighthouse-audit.yml
ran checkout then Lighthouse with no build step, while staticDistDir points at
./public -- which is gitignored (.gitignore:47) and untracked, so it did not exist
in the runner. Every URL 404'd and LHCI failed at `collect` on every run it ever had.
The workflow now builds first; these assertions are what the built artifact actually
measures.
URLS. Only a page a SIGNED-OUT visitor can actually render is audited. dashboard.html
was listed here and was never audited: its report came back with finalUrl
/account.html, because bg.js redirects an unauthenticated visitor off every gated
page. Auditing a gated page without an auth stub measures the login page instead.
NO PRESET. `lighthouse:recommended` was asserted here and cannot pass on this
architecture -- measured 2026-09-06, it failed on unminified-javascript,
unminified-css and unused-javascript (this project has no build step or bundler by
deliberate design -- CLAUDE.md section 9 and vercel.json), and on is-crawlable (the
platform is intentionally noindex and invitation-only). Those are assertions about a
pipeline this project has chosen not to have, not defects. Categories are asserted
explicitly instead.
ONLY ACCESSIBILITY IS ENFORCED, and that is a measurement, not modesty. Of the four
categories, accessibility is the only one that returned a number on every run here
(96 on index.html, 100 on account.html, 2026-09-06). The other three came back NULL,
for environment reasons rather than low quality: performance nulls when Chrome
collects no screenshots ('Chrome didn't collect any screenshots during the page
load') on these near-black pages, and best-practices nulls when the charset audit
hits 'Protocol error (Network.getResponseBody)'. A null score fails a minScore
assertion outright, so enforcing those categories makes the gate fail on harness
variance instead of on site quality. They are set to warn/off and still published on
every run.
0.9 is a RATCHET against a measured 96/100 floor: raise it as the site improves,
never lower it to make a run pass. If performance and best-practices start returning
stable numbers on the CI runner, enforce them too -- at whatever they actually
measure. One real signal that blocks is worth more than four that fail at random.
ONE URL, and that is a reliability measurement. With the build step in place the job
finally loaded and audited the pages on GitHub's runner -- and then failed a
different way: PROTOCOL_TIMEOUT on the TapTargets and ImageElements gatherers, and
'Waiting for DevTools protocol response has exceeded the allotted time' on
Runtime.evaluate and CSS.enable. The logs show why: this page injects ~59 inline
stylesheets (CLAUDE.md section 4.1 measures 62 sheets on a rendered page), Lighthouse
logs 'Error fetching content of stylesheet with URL ""' once per sheet, and Chrome's
CSS domain times out under it.
Measured 2026-09-06, auditing three URLs in one invocation: one pass, one
PROTOCOL_TIMEOUT failure, one hang killed at 400s, plus the failure on GitHub's
runner. Auditing one URL: three runs, three passes, zero protocol timeouts. So this
audits index.html alone -- the front door, and the highest-value public page. A
narrower gate that means something beats a wider one that fails at random. Add URLs
back when the stylesheet count comes down, not before.
CHROME FLAGS: --no-sandbox --disable-dev-shm-usage --disable-gpu are ordinary
container hardening and are kept on their own merits. They were tried FIRST as the
fix for the timeouts above and were NOT it -- the identical PROTOCOL_TIMEOUT
reproduced locally with them set. The page count was the variable that mattered.
KNOWN AND NOT HIDDEN: performance measured 0.34 on index.html in the one run that did
collect screenshots, and the recommended preset surfaced real defects worth their own
work -- aria-prohibited-attr, errors-in-console and label-content-name-mismatch.
Those are open findings, not things this config is papering over.
